answer.label: Not John Lennon — an anonymous internet anecdote
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · earliest full version documented 12 November 2008
answer.sourceLine: No book, interview, letter or recording of John Lennon has ever been shown to contain this story. Quote Investigator ↗ investigated it in 2013 and concluded there is no substantive evidence attaching the story to Lennon; the earliest full version it located is an anonymous Tumblr post dated 12 November 2008, which carried no attribution at all.

source.excerpt: When I was 5 years old, my mother always told me that happiness was the key to life. When I went to school, they asked me what I wanted to be when I grew up. I wrote down ‘happy’. They told me I didn’t understand the assignment, and I told them they didn’t understand life.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ investigated the anecdote on 29 May 2013 and concluded that there is no substantive evidence attaching the story to John Lennon. The earliest full version it located is a Tumblr post dated 12 November 2008, which QI notes carried no attribution.
Wikiquote’s John Lennon page ↗ — a dense, citation-heavy collection of his sourced remarks — does not contain this anecdote anywhere on it.

The nearest documented ancestors are a Peanuts strip of 11 January 1960 in which Linus answers “Outrageously happy!”, and Goldie Hawn’s own retelling in Vanity Fair in March 1992 and in her 2005 memoir A Lotus Grows in the Mud ↗. QI calls any influence on the modern anecdote speculative ↗.
The chronology alone is decisive: Lennon died on 8 December 1980 ↗, almost twenty-eight years before the earliest full version of this story that anyone has been able to document.
source.excerptNote: The line circulates in many small variants — the age changes, the tense changes, the closing sentence gets trimmed. There is no fixed authorial text to compare against, because no authored original has ever been produced.

source.rightsNote: The wording has no identifiable author and no first-publication anchor: its earliest documented appearance is an anonymous 2008 Tumblr post with no name attached. With no authored source work to date, no copyright status can be responsibly asserted — and it is certainly not public domain merely because its origin is unknown.

author.name: John Lennon
author.heading: About the man it gets pinned on
author.metaLine: 1940–1980 · English musician & songwriter · co-founder of the Beatles
author.bio: John Winston Ono Lennon was born in Liverpool on 9 October 1940 and shot dead in New York on 8 December 1980. He founded the Beatles, shared the era’s most famous songwriting partnership with Paul McCartney, and spent his solo years as an outspoken peace activist — a combination that made him one of the internet’s most reliable magnets for unsourced feel-good wisdom. He is heavily documented: hundreds of hours of interviews, several books, and a Wikiquote page dense with cited lines. This anecdote appears in none of them.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Lennon
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared “John Lennon” quotations online, and one of the least supported. The credit is late, undocumented, and contradicted by the only serious investigation of the story.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ states there is no substantive evidence attaching the story to Lennon, and documents no dated instance of anyone crediting him. Wikiquote’s John Lennon page ↗ does not list the anecdote at all — not as sourced, not as disputed, not as misattributed.

QI records a Peanuts strip of 11 January 1960 ↗ in which Linus answers the ‘what do you want to be’ question with “Outrageously happy!” — the kernel of the idea, but not this wording, and QI explicitly calls any influence on the later anecdote speculative.

Hawn told a version about her own childhood in Vanity Fair in March 1992 and again in her 2005 memoir A Lotus Grows in the Mud, as documented by QI ↗. QI does not identify her as the originator of the anonymous version that circulates under Lennon’s name.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: nobody knows who wrote it. Per Quote Investigator ↗, the earliest full version on record is an unattributed Tumblr post dated 12 November 2008 — almost twenty-eight years after John Lennon died.

context.heading: Why this one travelled so far
lead: The anecdote is built to be shared. It has a child, an institution, a one-word answer, and a closing line that lets the reader side with the child — the exact shape that survives being retyped into a caption. Attaching it to John Lennon costs nothing and adds everything: a name that already stands for gentle defiance of authority, and a man who cannot be asked.

The story also has genuine ancestors, which is part of why it feels older than it is. Quote Investigator ↗ records a Peanuts strip of 11 January 1960 in which Linus answers the grown-up question with “Outrageously happy!”, and Goldie Hawn telling a version about her own childhood in Vanity Fair in March 1992 and again in her 2005 memoir. QI is careful to call any influence on the modern anecdote speculative — these are precursors, not the source.
context.pull: The kernel is real and old. The wording, the schoolteacher, and the Lennon byline are not.
